records.name: North Korea
records.summary: North Korea is a place trans visitors should avoid entirely: same-sex conduct is not named in the Criminal Code, but Article 193 prohibits “decadent culture,” and broad obscene-activities provisions give the authorities unlimited discretion, and reported incidents of criminalisation and even execution for homosexuality exist. Gender identity does not exist in public life, visitors travel under constant escort and surveillance in the world's most totalitarian system, and any nonconforming presentation or discovered digital material risks detention, with no recorded protection or recognition of gender identity to offset that exposure.

sources.summary: Outright International country page (updated 12 Mar 2026): DPRK Criminal Code (1950, rev. 2009) appears to contain no penalty for consensual same-sex acts, but Art. 193 bans import/keeping/distribution of 'decadent culture' incl. sexual recordings and Art. 262 bans collective 'obscene activities'; 2014 KCNA denied homosexuality's existence; an openly gay defector published an autobiography in 2017; no documented state or non-state violence against LGBTIQ people; no registration route for LGBTI orgs.

Legal Clarity overview: sex-marker change on birth certificate/citizen card technically possible under 'unavoidable circumstances' - application to People's Security Agency plus state forensic medical evaluation, in practice requiring surgical intervention; no law explicitly bans gender-affirming care but the under-resourced health system makes hormones/surgery effectively inaccessible.

BBC Korean feature (10 Oct 2024), 'Does homosexuality exist in North Korea too?': 10 years after the UN COI report, new laws (Pyongyang Cultural Protection Act etc.) tighten control; profiles Jang Young-jin, a novelist who defected in the late 1990s and was forcibly outed, as the first publicly known gay defector; documents how a collective-over-individual regime forces DPRK sexual minorities into silent self-suppression and frames LGBT life as human-rights abuse.

US State Department 2022 Human Rights Report for North Korea: official assessment - the totalitarian regime's pervasive abuses; the report notes no specific law criminalising same-sex conduct but the regime's total control leaves no space for LGBT life.

US State Department 2020 Human Rights Report for North Korea: official assessment - no reliable information on LGBT persons; the regime's repression of all civil society is the dominant human-rights reality.
CNN (Apr 2017): 'I could not even dream: Life as a gay North Korean' — a defector's account of homosexuality's place in North Korean society and its punishment.

KCNA commentary (22 Apr 2014): state news agency rejects the UN Commission of Inquiry's DPRK human rights report as a political fabrication and personally attacks commissioner Michael Kirby as 'a disgusting old lecher with a 40-odd-year-long career of homosexuality' to discredit it - official-record evidence of the regime's hostility toward homosexuality even while denying its existence.

records.name: Palestinian Territories
records.summary:
Trans visitors face grave danger here, with a hard internal split: in the West Bank, same-sex conduct is not criminalised (Jordan's 1951 revision dropped consensual-private-sex offences, carried into the 1960 penal code applied there), but there are no protections, family/clan hostility is severe, and the Palestinian Authority has not legislated or signed key treaties. In the other part, Gaza, a 1936 British Mandate code technically allows up to 10 years for consensual same-sex acts, Hamas has executed people for alleged homosexuality, and the area is in a catastrophic war.

Trans identities are nowhere explicitly criminalised, but public-morality provisions can catch trans people, gender-affirming healthcare is essentially destroyed or unavailable, police action against a queer organisation drew rights-group condemnation, and periodic transphobic threats and attacks are reported.

sources.summary: CAIRO 51 Palestine page: Gaza (British Mandate Criminal Code Ordinance No. 74 of 1936 still in force, silent on trans identities but trans people potentially caught by public-morality provisions) vs West Bank have different penal codes; pinkwashing critique - occupation marginalises queer/trans Palestinians alongside everyone else; documented de facto oppression.

Legal Clarity: West Bank criminal law derives from the Jordanian Penal Code No. 16 of 1960 - Jordan's 1951 revision dropped consensual-private-sex offences and the 1960 code carried that forward; practical reality harsher than formal law via social/family persecution. Formal-decognition map for West Bank.

Wikipedia LGBT rights in Palestine: patchwork decriminalisation (British Mandate code in Jordan until 1951; Jordanian Penal Code no prohibition of same-sex acts applied to the West Bank; Israel stopped using the code in 1977); PA has not legislated; no explicit prohibition on trans identity; periodic transphobic threats/attacks; PA a non-signatory to key treaties.

HRW 'Audacity of Adversity' (16 Apr 2018): LGBT people across MENA finding ways to speak out - stories, cross-border alliances, national/regional movements combating homophobia and transphobia; accompanies AFE video series of activist messages of support. Regional movement context for Palestinian LGBT life.

Times of Israel: rights groups slammed Palestinian police for banning LGBTQ activity - after the police action against al-Qaws, the foundation received a wave of hate messages which activists said 'pose a serious threat' to the gay community.

HRW (11 Jun 2018), Women's Centre for Legal Aid: interviewed 12 Palestinian women identifying as lesbian/bisexual/queer - widespread discrimination and abuse in public and family settings; Gaza's 1936 Criminal Code s.152(2) punishes consensual same-sex 'carnal knowledge' by up to 10 years (vague 'unnatural offences' concepts violate privacy/non-discrimination per HRW); 1960 West Bank code analysed similarly.

Times of Israel: Israel to allow LGBT Palestinians granted temporary asylum to work - some 90 LGBT Palestinians have received temporary permits to seek refuge in Israel after fleeing violence in the territories.

records.name: Sierra Leone
records.summary: Sierra Leone is dangerous for trans visitors. The 1861 Offences Against the Person Act criminalises buggery with up to life imprisonment (men only) — enforcement is limited but discrimination and violence are regular; no LGR; a small community organises quietly.

sources.summary: NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403); the underlying Human Dignity Trust country profile documents Sierra Leone's criminalisation of same-sex activity (up to life imprisonment under the 1861 Offences Against the Person Act).

Amnesty International Sierra Leone 2025 country report (LGBTI section): consensual sexual relations between women are not explicitly outlawed, but lesbian women face significant social, cultural and economic barriers to living freely — stigma, harassment, and limited acceptance from families and communities; no non-discrimination protection for SOGI is documented.

Joint ICCPR shadow report (March 2014) to the UN Human Rights Committee: 'Breaking the Silence on Human Rights Violations in Sierra Leone' - discrimination and violence based on SOGI; covers civil-war sexual violence, discrimination in health and education, hate speech by religious institutions, and hate crimes against LGBTI human-rights defenders.

US State Department 2012 Human Rights Report for Sierra Leone: documents police killings, corruption, FGM/C, and 'official and societal discrimination against lesbian, gay, bisexual, and transgender (LGBT) individuals'.

GlobalGayz news archive for Sierra Leone (Richard Ammon, items dated 2004-2010): records the November 2004 rape and murder of lesbian activist FannyAnn Eddy, the January 2005 arrest of her killer, police refusal to classify it as a hate crime, and the alleged murderer's reported escape from custody in July 2005 — dated evidence on violence against LGBT activists and the justice response.

records.name: Kosovo
records.summary: Kosovo is workable for trans visitors — the Balkans' strongest legal framework on paper. The constitution (Art 24) bans discrimination based on sexual orientation; the 2015 Law on Protection from Discrimination covers gender identity; legal gender recognition is possible (medicalised); and the government attempted same-sex unions in 2024 as part of Council of Europe accession. Counterweights: implementation is inconsistent, political hate speech is common (2022 CSGD report: year marked by intolerance), and Pristina Pride proceeds under protection.

sources.summary: Outright overview (upd. Mar 2026): constitutional ban on SO discrimination (art. 24) plus the 2015 Law on Protection from Discrimination covering gender identity — but implementation inconsistent; PM Kurti's April 2024 pledge to legalise same-sex civil unions stalled, and as of Feb 2026 Parliament still failed to adopt the new Civil Code amid fierce opposition including from the ruling party.
NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 401); the underlying Reuters report (May 2024) covers Muslim-majority Kosovo considering same-sex unions amid fierce opposition.

ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2024 (covering 2023) chapter on Kosovo: PM Kurti said during Pride week he would 'do his utmost' to get the Civil Code adopted (2022 parliament had voted against same-sex-couple recognition amendments); a Justice Ministry working group was drafting a bill; CSGD's 2022 annual report found intolerance and hatred, with politicians' hate speech common during Civil Code debates; an artist received death threats over a painting; Kosovo Pride Week held with the motto 'I love you as you are!'.

Prishtina Insight (Jan 2019): ECtHR ruled Macedonia's surgery requirement for gender-marker change violates private-life rights (X v FYROM); Kosovo's Blert Morina — who has his own Constitutional Court case on name/gender change on Kosovo IDs — watched the ruling closely, documenting that Kosovo's legal gender recognition route ran through the courts at that time.
Euronews (March 2022): Kosovo's parliament rejected the new law recognising same-sex civil unions (page largely navigation content at fetch time).

Prishtina Insight: third annual Pride Parade in Prishtina, with week-long exhibitions, parties, conferences and discussions by the Center for Equality and Liberty (CEL) — slogan both an appeal for tolerance and an invitation to join the parade; visible, public LGBTI organising in the capital.

IntelliNews: 'Kosovo's new Civil Code opens the way for gay marriage' - analysis of the Civil Code's gender-neutral marriage language and its implications (page largely navigation content at fetch time).

records.name: Gibraltar
records.summary:
Gibraltar legislates its own civil and criminal law as a self-governing territory on the Iberian peninsula's southern tip. Same-sex activity has been legal since 1993 with an equal age of consent since 2012; discrimination protections covering sexual orientation and gender reassignment date from 2007; civil partnerships followed in 2014, and same-sex marriage was enacted unanimously in December 2016 after a 2015 public consultation returned overwhelming support (3,490 replies from a 24,117-person electorate).

For a transgender visitor the standing gap is legal gender: no route exists to change legal gender, and there was no specific hate-crime provision denigrating a person for sexual orientation until, in July 2021, the Ministry for Justice said it would 'urgently' consider one after a wave of online homophobia during Pride month drew a rare public rebuke from the head of government. Governance of the territory is subject to regular scrutiny by the UK parliament's overseas-territories committee, which has pressed accountability standards across the portfolio.

sources.summary: UK House of Commons Foreign Affairs Committee, Seventh Report (2007-08) on Overseas Territories: governance chapter - covers good-governance expectations, corruption concerns (Turks and Caicos), and accountability issues across the territories including Gibraltar.

El País in English (15 Aug 2016): Gibraltar put a draft bill amending the Civil Marriage Act for same-sex marriage before Parliament after a December 2015 consultation that left Gibraltarians polarized; a government minister presided over an inter-ministerial committee weighing all viewpoints, with popular consultation and main parties suggesting support for the change.

Gibraltar Chronicle (22 Jul 2021): the Ministry for Justice and Equality said it would 'urgently' consider legislation to tackle 'disgusting lurking homophobia' following an incident of anti-gay abuse.

Wikiwand (Wikipedia mirror): LGBTQ rights in Gibraltar - legal since 1993, equal age of consent since 2012, adoption right by Supreme Court ruling 2013, civil partnerships since 2014, same-sex marriage since Dec 2016 (passed unanimously), discrimination protections for sexual orientation and 'gender reassignment' since 2007; transgender persons not allowed to change legal gender.

records.name: Bermuda
records.summary:
Bermuda decriminalised private adult same-sex conduct in 1994 (House of Assembly, 22-16) and in 2013 outlawed discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation. Same-sex marriages performed in 2017 were withdrawn the following year by a Domestic Partnership Act — the first jurisdiction anywhere to reverse marriage equality — and in March 2022 the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council upheld that restoration of the traditional-marriage definition, so partnerships, not marriage, are the available status for same-sex couples.

For a transgender visitor the more telling fact is the protection gap: there is no legal recognition of transgender people, and therefore no gender-identity-specific discrimination protection at all. Church influence is significant in local politics — when a prominent entertainer's gay-charity cruise sought to dock in 2007 the premier's colourful defence was needed against religious objections — and the tourism economy that the island depends on has repeatedly had to be pointed at inclusivity.

sources.summary: Bernews (Feb 2018): Bermuda's Governor gave assent to the Domestic Partnership Act 2017, replacing same-sex marriage with domestic partnerships for both same-sex and heterosexual couples - the reversal that made Bermuda the first jurisdiction to revoke marriage equality.

Social climate: Bermuda's AME and other churches protested a gay cruise (Norwegian Dawn, New York–Bermuda, July 12) as 'incompatible with the word of God and the Christian moral fibre' — organised religious hostility to visible same-sex couples.

LGBTQ Nation/AP (July 2013): Bermuda's Senate passed the Human Rights Amendment Act outlawing discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation (also banning age discrimination); same-sex marriage not then permitted.

Royal Gazette (14 May 1994): the House of Assembly voted 22–16 to decriminalise consensual sex between adult men, removing two Criminal Code sections — a debate that split the island, with religious leaders divided and the Christian Coalition staging marches against it.
